findings_and_limits: All 537 supplied viewer pages have text reading checkpoints, including notes, captions, tables, chapter references and the locus index. The B2 reservoir was only partly excavated. Its minimum capacity and inferred original construction cannot establish an observed connection to the other water installations. Pottery beneath the collapsed roof dates its last use and provides a terminus for collapse.

The chapter author and book editors disagree about whether the garden and foundation trenches were contemporary. Tunnel 10181 is secondary, and its opening into Pool 6 was subsequently plastered shut while the pool continued in use.
Trench 6020 is reassessed as an earlier water feature beneath later Wall C29; a covered channel and an open pool remain alternatives. The previously published Pool 3 identification is withdrawn.

Pool 1 retains three chronological scenarios. Gutter 1 reaches an irregular breach in Channel A, so its present connection need not belong to the initial garden phase. The sealing of Gutter 4 was removed during the 2012 reconstruction (figure 7.29).
The floor of cistern 832 was not reached. The bottom line at 814.47 in section 7.44 represents the excavation limit and cannot supply the ancient storage depth.

Sections 6.22 and 6.23 label the channel 11040, while the photographs, Table 6.3 and prose call it 10040. Figure 5.3 contains printed elevations 860.78/860.41 amid 815–816 m levels. Preserve the mismatches rather than silently repairing them.
The early and revised coordinate frames differ between figures 4.8 and 5.1. No coordinate transformation is established here.

The D1 installations include tentative bath identifications and later reservoir conversion. Installation 13069 was entered through a breach and was not excavated; its function remains unknown. Space 472 is interpreted as storage or hiding rather than securely as a cistern.

Table 9.4 assigns locus 473 to square D428, while plan 9.57 places it in the D227–D228 area. Space 472 has little surviving plaster; its photographs show the opening and roofed interior but do not establish a cistern function.

The previously proposed inner gate is redated to the Early Roman period. Bathhouse and church phasing includes unresolved caption/table disagreements; the proposed earthquake association remains tentative.

Area D4 retains two eastern fortification reconstructions: a partly unexposed casemate system or a single massive wall. The relationship of Walls D542–D543 to the courtyard and northern fortification remains unresolved. Wall D589 was damaged by later cistern construction and its foundations were unexcavated.

Phase D4-6 groups walls that need not be contemporary. Only D546 and D538 have independent dating evidence; D540 may belong to D4-6, D4-5 or D4-4. The Roman villa construction date rests on stylistic comparison, and the proposed fountain function remains tentative.

Printed pages 284 and 292 reverse the D76/D96 assignments of robber loci 12041 and 12043. Figure 12.30 names D509 in its caption while the preceding account discusses D569; the photograph labels both. Figure 12.31 assigns Kiln 15257 to D4-1, whereas printed page 325 assigns it to D4-2 and distinguishes the modern D4-1 bunker that cuts it. Preserve these source conflicts.

Printed pages 308, 322 and 323 use BCE for agricultural or church construction dates where the surrounding chronology and other passages use CE. Figure 12.56 captions Floor 286 while the photograph and prose identify Floor 268. Figure 13.9 assigns Wall D120 to D6-5 while the detailed text assigns it to D6-4. The published variants remain explicit.

In Area D6, the excavators dismantled a cement restoration of Wall Wh89. They retain a later Byzantine construction proposal beside Solimani’s Late Hellenistic interpretation and acknowledge a possible older wall suggested by a small bedrock ledge. The standing display cannot alone establish the ancient phase.

The Iron Age assignments of Walls D52, D117 and D125 depend mainly on masonry style. Their construction contexts were absent or previously exposed; the D117–D52 junction was destroyed or unresolved. Cave 14204 has unknown function and a tentative phase; Installation 14203 has an unresolved connection to the nearby water features.

The pipe beneath Vat 15184 was detected but not exposed. The text gives inconsistent directions for the lead pipe between vats 276 and 277. Several underground installations retain unknown function, date or hidden floors.

The twin baths include incomplete exterior basins and uncertain approaches. The southern columbarium has later filling and new floors; several entrances are sealed or damaged, and Passage H is unfinished or of uncertain destination. The coin hoard does not prove a particular hiding-event reconstruction.

Terrace samples include medieval, early modern and nineteenth-century results. They do not date every terrace to one episode. Garden areas and rainfall/storage estimates differ between summaries and detailed descriptions.

Viewer 355 (printed 344) describes Cistern 14206 as unexplored beneath Slabs 14112. The approximately 380 coins on Pavement 14013 supply the published late fifth/early sixth-century CE terminus post quem for D6-5; they do not expose the cistern construction. Figure 13.20 calls D118 D6-4, while the earlier building account and Plan 13.19 include it in D6-5 with later piers.

Floor 14131 is 818.69 m in the initial printed 347 statement, but 818.63 m later on that page and in Plan 13.25. Floors 14128 and 14131 could span D6-5/D6-4 or belong to one phase. Agricultural reuse in D6-2 is inferred. Locus 14111 is called a cistern in D6-3 and a pit in D6-2.

The subterranean survey distinguishes twelve openings from underground complexes: Ug5 and Ug7 lead to one columbarium. Ug1 has a sediment-covered floor and an unexplained western breach. Ug8 has apparently modern mortar over earlier plaster. Ug11 has a seventh-century coin within a coating layer; this dates the coating subject to its construction history, rather than independently dating the rock-cutting.

Ug4, Ug6 and Ug9 retain unknown function and date. Ug9 access could be ancient or a modern military trench. Ug12 was not fully excavated, its floor was hidden, and cellar/storage function and phase attribution remain tentative. Cave plans show surviving surveyed spaces and present deposit surfaces.

RR8 and RR9 preserve only two segments of the original exterior basin; its complete outline and eastern approach are reconstructed. A late Hasmonean coin in RR8 floor substructure gives a terminus post quem, while construction could be first century BCE or CE. Post-70 CE objects in RR9 date dumping; abandonment during the Great Revolt is tentative. Later D123 was partly dismantled for excavation; lost superstructure support and RR8 storage reuse are interpretations.

Viewer 386 references Table 15.1; its actual cells and Table 15.2 were inspected at viewer 388. Table 15.2 retains six proposed phases, Ug7-6 earliest to Ug7-1 modern. The Southern Columbarium chronology has four dated anchors and remains a general assessment where individual phases lack dates.

Plans 15.4, 15.8, 15.22 and 15.27, Sections 15.5a-c and their enlarged native crops distinguish exposed early spaces, dashed reconstructed limits, later architecture and unexcavated portions. The early floor at 810.30 m belongs to the limited northwestern probe. Figure 15.4 literally captions Phases Ug-7 and Ug-6, whereas Table 15.2 assigns the early columbarium to Ug7-6; printed 376 cites Figure 15.6 for the northwestern exposure, while the actual Figure 15.6 caption identifies the southeastern edge.

The early columbarium date relies on its proposed relation to the later Hasmonean replacement, without direct construction or use debris. Later construction fills include mixed Iron Age, Persian and Hellenistic sherds; their interpretation as imported deliberate fills does not establish an observed source in above-ground ruins. Locus 16018 is only possibly equivalent to 16025, and excavation there stopped below the C37 foundation.

The late floor and support walls provide local relative sequences, including a later lintel inserted into an existing niche. Unit B was excavated only in its northern half, and its complete walls and fill were not exposed. Locus 885 has two retained interpretations: deliberate wall-associated fill or a later dump after ceiling loss. Its use as a terminus for Ug7-4 depends on the preferred first interpretation. Most of Chamber E ceiling was removed during excavation for safety.

Pit G was sealed by slabs and jar fragments and contained only a thin eroded chalk layer. Passage H ends abruptly after a short eastern extension; its destination and function remain unknown. A hideout interpretation depends on typological resemblance, and the authors explicitly report no direct functional evidence. The hoard of fifteen Tyrian shekels has latest coins dated 11/10 BCE, a terminus for caching; its connection to Chamber F modification remains speculative. The overfloor accumulation may record additional activities or later pigeon nesting.

The Late Roman dumps interfingered between two shafts, preventing precise locus boundaries and cross-quadrant correlations. Glass waste and proposed sewage layers are separately described; their functions are not interchangeable. Chamber D has a modern military breach and lost ancient floor, while the modern opening toward Chamber F may have been made by other visitors or excavators.

Figure 16.2 maps GPS/ArcGIS survey observations on a bounded western-slope orthophoto with a north arrow, 100 m scale and feature legend. No coordinate grid, CRS or positional error is supplied. The approximately seven-hectare survey was bounded by modern construction and cultivated plots; the no-habitation inference is limited to that study area.

Western-slope basin photographs show isolated rock cuts, including one beneath a terrace. Their proposed hewn-vineyard function is a cautious typological inference. Quarrying and basin cuts partly predate terraces, but their exact individual construction dates remain unresolved. The cistern, drawn-water channel and small Type IV plot are linked in the published account; vegetable growing is proposed.

OSL profile photographs and Figure 16.24 preserve sampled sediment ages separately from terrace-construction interpretations. The rank-order chart uses years before 2010, calendar CE and an axis break; its three very old samples belong to underlying natural soils. T1, T7 and T12 West show depth-order deviations. Type II original construction versus later inner-row addition remains unresolved, and Wall T2 gives different ages in separate probes.

The 1945 and 1973 aerials, excavation photographs, 1993 geodesy and development plan record different modern terrain states. Excavation dumps and military works altered the hill; the military plan included works that were never constructed. Aharoni draft Figure 17.6 has explicitly incorrect absolute elevations. The reduced geodesy has resolution and missing-coverage limits.

Figure 17.9 locates six backhoe soundings with north arrow, 50 m scale and numeric grid but without a named CRS. Sections 17.10-17.13 distinguish fill, modern dump and bedrock. Printed page 444 refers to Figure 7.12 for Sounding C6, whose actual section is Figure 17.12. The C1 sounding was defeated by modern development, and several garden boundaries remain reconstructed.

Figure 17.14 labels the reconstructed natural summit 820.10 m, while printed page 446 reports 819.85 m. Figure 17.15 draws A-A west-east and B-B north-south, while captions 17.16 and 17.17 reverse those direction descriptions. Preserve the variants. Faint building and wall lines in the sections are explicitly reconstructed; interpolated terrain is distinct from directly exposed rock points.

Plans 17.19, 18.1, 18.2, 18.3 and 20.1 are native-inspected phase syntheses. They distinguish rock treatment, pools, trenches, channels, gutters and dashed extensions; their combined phases do not prove that every feature operated simultaneously. Figures 17.20-17.23 and 18.4 are terrain, palace or vegetation reconstructions, with superstructure and planting inferred.

The northern and southern installation plans were inspected at viewer 473-474 with enlarged crops. The roughly 400 cubic metre storage figure is explicitly based on secure documented installations; the unexcavated assumed northwestern reservoir is additional. The rainfall estimate remains modeled, and the chapter explicitly acknowledges presumed as well as observed connections.

The reduced archival order and map have resolution-limited fine labels. Their planned fortifications must be separated from constructed features and ancient rock-cut installations.

Printed 27-30 (viewer 28-31) uses a reservoir threshold above 50 cubic metres or a non-bell shape, while the cited Tsuk definition uses 100 cubic metres. Covered drinking-water and open irrigation functions are proposals; temporary wood or hide roofs remain possible.

Consumption assumptions differ by paper. The introduction at printed 33-35 (viewer 34-36) uses 7 litres per person daily, approximately 2.5 cubic metres yearly; the third paper deliberately selects 7 cubic metres yearly; Environmental Archaeology uses 3 cubic metres yearly; the IEJ discussion uses 5 cubic metres yearly and its siege calculation uses 5 litres daily. Keep these branches separate from estimated population and surplus.

Viewer 37-43 preserves coordinate conflicts between Table 2 and site descriptions, including identical table coordinates for Deir Qala and Deir Dakla. The expanded study selected preserved sites where new contribution was feasible; its inventory does not establish regional rarity. Political or military purpose rests on historical and architectural interpretation.

IEJ 73 pages 56-72 (viewer 56-72) reconstructs el-Hamam slope capacities of 450, 500 and 650 cubic metres from partly silt-filled chambers. The summit estimate of 340 cubic metres assumes an original depth of 7-8 m beyond surviving height; the expanded Hebrew article at viewer 164 instead reports 200 cubic metres plus 7 for the channel. Channel length is 7 m in IEJ and 8 m in the expanded article. Published slope totals include 1600, 1650 and 1700 cubic metres, and the expanded overall prose uses about 2100; do not harmonize them.

The el-Hamam inverted siphon, western collapsed entrance, earlier ramp and guard structure remain reconstructions. The successful slope-reservoir result is OxA-41307, 2115 +/- 19 BP, with a 95.4 percent interval of 2145-2001 calibrated BP; the acknowledgement names Beta Analytic instead. The expanded article note 34 at viewer 176 reports failed summit radiocarbon sampling because organic remains were absent. Summit Iron Age attribution remains analogy and historical inference.

The expanded Hebrew article at viewer 169-170 proposes a 67 CE siege by the fifteenth legion, while viewer 176 returns to 66 CE. IEJ and other dissertation sections also retain 66/67 alternatives. Soldier numbers, siege duration, protected water and hidden access derive historical reconstructions; slope water outside the wall had acknowledged access risk.

Environmental Archaeology viewer 74-86 records modern rain and reservoir levels, with 2021 graph labels differing from prose abbreviations and a separately reported 2021-22 observation. Full ancient fill, reconstructed roof catchment, crop use and imperial strategy remain inferences. The measured storage inventory, reconstructed roofs and modeled surplus are separate quantities.

Third-paper viewer 89-128 gives table/prose capacity differences for Sam’an and Dakla. Dakla about 3000 cubic metres includes a former wine-pit complex. al-Arab channel drainage differs from an earlier filling-channel interpretation; its depth was unexcavated. Matching plaster does not independently date all reservoirs to the same episode.

The third-paper radiocarbon appendix at viewer 117 retains the actual al-Arab reservoir 2 ranges of 591-661 and 584-658 CE at 95.4 percent. The author also writes 580-640 and narrows to 580-590; those historical selections are not new measurements. Sam’an 5 has a modern 1951-1959 result and El Mir 1 a broad 405-1030 CE result. Dakla 5 and Dakla 1 have different multi-interval results and low-carbon limits; carbon age alone need not establish plaster application.

The winery article at viewer 132-149 has correctly checked northern A and southern B hill labels. Its pit chronology and preferred wine function depend on typological comparison; local floors are hidden by silt and no collected pottery dates the cuts. Reservoir 7 is plastered in the table and earlier account, while later prose calls reservoir 1 plastered; retain the discrepancy.

Mount Ebal viewer 182-204 has three actual samples: Beta-621033 at 2020 +/- 30 BP, Beta-621032 at 1040 +/- 30 BP and Beta-621031 at 880 +/- 30 BP. Native calibration plots and layer labels were checked, but an exact calibrated endpoint table is absent. Their broad periods are first century BCE/CE, tenth/eleventh CE and twelfth/thirteenth CE. Seed and sediment photo cross-references are reversed in the bullets. The later dissertation summary calls four dated periods and Late Roman; it does not replace the three embedded-paper records.

The Mount Ebal text gives New Israeli Grid 227750/679351, outside the native Figure 2 extent of E227240-227460/N682740-682880. Published 42 cubic metres does not follow directly from the stated 7.7 by 5.5 by 2.5 m chamber or its reconstructed 5.5 m depth. No corrected coordinate or capacity was invented. An earlier unplastered pit and relation to the cultic enclosure remain unproved; Byzantine disuse and pastoral ownership are hypotheses.

Discussion Table 4 at viewer 212 mixes relative/analogical and radiocarbon dates, gives Iron II eighth/seventh-century CE as printed, calls the al-Arab sample site 1B instead of reservoir 2 and extrapolates sampled plaster ages to undated sites. Its basal layer 0 differs from layer 1 in the Ebal article. Modern optimized grape irrigation is explicitly an unproved proposal at viewer 210 note 2.

Appendix tables and native plans/photos at viewer 219-229 report Gerizim four features totaling 601 cubic metres, Hemed four totaling 517.4 and El Mir five totaling 127.35. Box-product capacities in bell-shaped or rubble-filled spaces require their stated limits. Hemed feature 1 northing 665010 differs from the other features at 666xxx.
